Hearing no opposition, approval of the minutes is passed. Now we're going to move on to information items.

Tonight we're going-- or this afternoon, we're going to revisit Policy 8650: Student Technology and Acceptable Responsible Use. And we have a presentation, so if you'd like to begin, that would be fine. Excellent. So thank you. Tonight, we are bringing updates to Policy 8650: Student Technology Acceptable Responsible Use. The proposed revisions to Policy 8650 update and modernize the student technology

acceptable use policy by clarifying technology monitoring and content filtering practices, incorporating some digital citizenship instruction information, addressing responsible use of emerging technologies such as generative AI, and making minor editorial changes. References to technology resources have been expanded. We do not have mainframes anymore, so we removed some of the legacy terminology and updated it to better reflect what we actually provide and what we do. Language in the monitoring section was revised to clarify that usage and

activity on LCPS technology systems are monitored. Communications may be backed up, and security tools may be employed to maintain the integrity and security of the network. The policy clarifies LCPS operates technology protection measures, such as to monitor, filter, and block inappropriate content on all devices connected to LCPS networks, including wireless networks. Student education requirements are updated to include digital citizenship, as I stated before. And there's new language that explicitly addresses responsible and

ethical use of emerging technologies. We included generative artificial intelligence as an example, but as those could-- we left it open-ended enough to address any technology that is emerging and could be incorporated into the policy. Just one note. Virginia Code 22.1-70.2 requires that this policy is updated every two years, so we're bringing it for its two-year review cycle. And after this conversation tonight, it'll be posted for public feedback during the

normal process, and I will be back with feedback to discuss it as an action item at the October 26th meeting. So with that, that's a summary of the policy changes, and I'm happy to take any questions. Ms. Donahue, go ahead. Thank you very much, Chair LaBelle. Thank you for that summary, Mr. Smith. My question, I'm not even sure if it's directly germane to this proposed policy

change, but I happened to be at an event yesterday, and I was talking to a student from Rock Ridge High School. And when I asked her, as I do anytime I have, wishing that they could use their MacBook, and knowing that that was not permissible under policy. So since you're here, is that correct, that it's against policy to allow students to use their personal devices? And assuming that that is correct, what is our reason for that particular restriction?

Sure. So this policy doesn't specifically cover that topic, but it is addressed in 8655, which is a partner policy to this, and that's the student personal device use policy. So basically, state law requires that students are not allowed to use any personal technology that connects to any internet and transfers any data between bell to bell. So that is a state law that was passed. And they actually updated it this previous year to make it even a little more

restrictive to change some of the language from restrict to ban. So there were some legal conversations about those having different meanings. So they tightened it and doubled down on no technology. Now, if there's an accommodation needed for 504 IEP, there's also for EL students. So that it really is because the state law.

So before the state law was put into place, we had a little bit more flexibility with that and we restricted K through eight, and we did allow high school students because they do have personal preference. If you made me work on a Mac, it would take me a little bit because I don't use one every single day. But if you take a Mac user and put them on a Chromebook, it's the same thing. So it's really the state law that's driving that for us. Thank you, Mr. Smith. That's very helpful to know, and I assume the state law that you're referring to is the one that colloquially I think of as the cellphone ban,

when the state moved to pass the code that does not allow use of cellphones. But to your point, it is broader than just cellphones. It includes any wearable tech, smartwatches, meta glasses, anything that transmits. And it really is the language in the policy. It's called a cellphone policy, but it's any technology that transfers data, and that's pretty much every piece of technology. So it's pretty much a ubiquitous ban, bell to bell.

Students are still allowed to use it before and after school or personally to do their homework and stuff like that. They just can't use it during class time. Thank you very much. That's very helpful. That's all I had, Chair LaBelle. Thank you. Thank you, Ms. Donahue. Do you have any questions, Mr. Swenson? No questions from me. Okay. Thank you very much. move this to go forward to our different groups that we have to send them out to? Is there a motion to do so? Well, we're not making a motion, right?

Typically, SVAC has made motions to send- I thought ... policies to public comment. Whether or not that is required, I can't say, but that is certainly our practice here at SVAC. Well, we'll cover all the bases. Yes. We'll cover all the bases this way. So moved. Thank you. Is there a second? Seconded. Thank you, Mr. Swenson. Forward. Thank you, Ms. Donahue.
